# SeaWindow: Tide Times & Charts

> Official website of SeaWindow, an iPhone app for tide times, tide charts and coastal weather, made by independent developer Mohamed Elatabany.

SeaWindow is an iPhone app (iOS 18 or later) that shows tide times and tide charts, hourly coastal weather, waves and swell, sea temperature, and sun and moon times for coasts worldwide. US tides come from NOAA CO-OPS predictions at more than 3,000 stations. Elsewhere SeaWindow uses open international tide-station data, calculated on the iPhone, or WorldTides predictions, and where no station is near, the EOT20 global tide model, labelled as an estimate. Weather comes from Apple Weather. Today's forecast and charts, a tide widget and one favorite coast are free; optional SeaWindow Pro adds ten days ahead, every chart for every day, annual tide tables, unlimited favorites, alerts, offline forecasts, all widgets, Live Activities and Apple Watch. No account, no ads, no tracking. It is a planning aid, not a navigation or safety tool.

App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6811683172

## Pages
## About SeaWindow

SeaWindow is made by one independent developer, Mohamed Elatabany. The app has no account and no advertising. Features listed on this site are checked against the app's source code and the live App Store listing. Prices are shown in the app and on the App Store, not on this website, because they vary by country.

## SeaWindow

https://seawindowtides.com/

Home page: what SeaWindow shows, free and Pro features, data sources and FAQ.

Q: Is SeaWindow free?
A: Yes. SeaWindow is free to download and shows today’s tide curve, the next high and low, today’s weather and charts, sun and moon times, one favorite coast and a current-tide widget at no cost. SeaWindow Pro is an optional weekly, monthly or yearly subscription that adds ten days ahead, annual tide tables, alerts, offline forecasts, all widgets and Apple Watch.

Q: Does SeaWindow work outside the United States?
A: Yes. In the US it uses NOAA predictions. Elsewhere it calculates tides on the iPhone from open international tide-station data or uses WorldTides predictions, and where no station is near, it uses the EOT20 global tide model and labels the result as an estimate. Places far up an estuary or inland have no tide data.

Q: Where do SeaWindow’s tide times come from?
A: US tide times are NOAA CO-OPS predictions for the station shown on screen. Outside the US they come from open tide-station constants calculated on the device, from WorldTides, or from the EOT20 model. The app shows the station, its distance, the provider and the datum for every coast.

Q: Does SeaWindow have widgets and an Apple Watch app?
A: Yes. The current-tide widget is free. SeaWindow Pro unlocks the other widgets (tide chart, tide table, wind, weather, sun, moon and a large dashboard), Live Activities and the Apple Watch app with complications.

Q: Can I use SeaWindow without a signal?
A: SeaWindow keeps the last forecast it loaded. With Pro you can download an offline forecast pack for a favorite coast before you head out; expired packs stay clearly labelled until you replace them.

Q: Do I need an account? Does SeaWindow track me?
A: No account is needed, and there are no ads, analytics or tracking. Your places and journal stay on your iPhone. Location is optional and only used to suggest a nearby coast.

Q: Can I use SeaWindow for navigation?
A: No. SeaWindow is a planning aid. Tide predictions do not include storm surge, wind set-up or river flow. For navigation and safety, use official charts, marine forecasts and warnings.

Q: Is SeaWindow available on iPad or Android?
A: SeaWindow is made for iPhone with iOS 18 or later, with an Apple Watch app. There is no Android version.

## Tide height calculator

https://seawindowtides.com/tide-calculator.html

Tide height calculator by SeaWindow. Rule of twelfths: the tide moves 1, 2, 3, 3, 2 and 1 twelfths of its range in the six equal parts between a low and a high (cumulative 1, 3, 6, 9, 11, 12 twelfths). The cosine method gives fraction = (1 − cos(π·t/T))/2. Worked example, NOAA station 9414290 San Francisco, 5 Nov 2026: low 0.862 ft at 1:47 AM, high 5.913 ft at 8:35 AM (MLLW); at 5:00 AM the cosine method gives 3.17 ft, the rule of twelfths 3.18 ft, NOAA's hourly prediction 3.06 ft. Estimates exclude weather; not for navigation.

Q: What is the rule of twelfths?
A: A rule of thumb for estimating tide height between a low and a high. Divide the time between them into six equal parts; the water moves 1/12, 2/12, 3/12, 3/12, 2/12 and 1/12 of the tidal range in those parts, so it is a quarter of the way after two parts and halfway after three.

Q: Is the rule of twelfths accurate?
A: On a regular semidiurnal tide it is usually within a few percent of the range. In the San Francisco example on this page it was within 0.16 ft of NOAA’s hourly predictions. It fails where the tide has an unusual shape, such as a double high water, and it never includes weather.

Q: What is the difference between the rule of twelfths and the cosine method?
A: The rule of twelfths is a stepwise approximation you can do in your head. The cosine method uses the smooth half-cosine shape of a tide between two extremes. They agree exactly after two, three and four sixths of the time and differ by at most about 2.6% of the range.

Q: Can I use this calculator for any tide station?
A: Yes. Enter two consecutive tides (a high and a low) from any tide table, in feet or metres. Use the station closest to where you will be, and remember that both methods assume a regular tide shape.

Q: Does the calculator store my data?
A: No. Everything is calculated in your browser. The share link only puts your numbers in the web address.

## How to read a tide chart

https://seawindowtides.com/how-to-read-a-tide-chart.html

A tide chart is a curve of predicted water height over time: peaks are high tides, dips are low tides, and every height is measured from a datum (MLLW at NOAA stations in the US). Worked example: NOAA station 9414290, San Francisco (Golden Gate), 5 November 2026: low 0.9 ft at 1:47 AM, high 5.9 ft at 8:35 AM, low 0.7 ft at 2:48 PM, high 4.7 ft at 9:03 PM (MLLW); mean sea level is 3.12 ft above MLLW there.

Q: What does a negative tide mean?
A: The water is predicted to fall below the datum. With NOAA’s MLLW datum, a reading such as −1.8 ft means 1.8 ft lower than the average of the lowest daily tides.

Q: Why are the two high tides different heights?
A: Many coasts, including the U.S. West Coast, have a mixed semidiurnal tide, where the two daily highs and lows differ in height.

Q: Why doesn’t the water at my beach match the chart?
A: The chart predicts the tide at one station without weather. Distance from the station, local geography, wind and air pressure all change what you see.

Q: Is a tide chart the same as a tide table?
A: A tide table lists the times and heights of highs and lows. The curve joins those points. NOAA reserves “tide chart” for maps of a bay, but most apps use it for the curve.

Q: How do I switch SeaWindow between feet and metres?
A: Open Settings with the gear button and choose ft or m under Tide height.

## Why tide times differ between apps and websites

https://seawindowtides.com/why-tide-times-differ.html

Tide times differ between sources mainly because they use different stations (a reference station or a subordinate station computed from it), a global tide model instead of a station, a different datum (MLLW, chart datum/LAT or mean sea level), a different time zone, or different rounding; weather then moves the real water away from every prediction. Worked example from NOAA predictions retrieved on November 19, 2026 for November 21, 2026: San Francisco (Golden Gate) 9414290 high 6.0 ft at 8:15 AM; Coyote Point Marina 9414449, a subordinate station 27 km away inside the bay, high 7.8 ft at 8:57 AM (NOAA offsets: highs +42 min and ×1.29, lows +68 min and ×1.01). The same 8:15 AM high is 6.0 ft above MLLW but 2.9 ft above mean sea level, and 16:15 in GMT.

Q: Which tide time should I trust?
A: The prediction for the station closest to you on the same stretch of water, from the official agency where possible (NOAA CO-OPS in the United States). Check the station and its distance first.

Q: Why is my tide time an hour off?
A: Usually daylight saving or a time zone mix-up: the same prediction can be listed in GMT, local standard time or local daylight time.

Q: Why do the heights differ when the times match?
A: The sources probably use different datums, such as MLLW, chart datum or mean sea level, or round differently. At San Francisco, a 6.0 ft high above MLLW is 2.9 ft above mean sea level.

Q: What is a subordinate tide station?
A: A station predicted by applying time differences and height ratios to a nearby reference station, such as Coyote Point Marina from San Francisco (Golden Gate).

Q: Does SeaWindow include storm surge?
A: No. SeaWindow shows astronomical tide predictions or model estimates, without storm surge or tidal currents. Check official marine forecasts and warnings for those.

## King tides 2026–2027: what they are and when to expect them

https://seawindowtides.com/king-tides.html

King tide is a popular, non-scientific name for the year’s highest tides, usually perigean spring tides, when a new or full moon falls close to the moon’s perigee (NOAA: typically six to eight times a year). The California King Tides Project lists November 24–26, 2026, December 23–25, 2026 and January 21–22, 2027 statewide (checked November 19, 2026). NOAA predictions for San Francisco 9414290, retrieved November 19, 2026: on December 24, 2026 a high of 7.2 ft at 10:37 AM and a low of −1.8 ft at 5:42 PM (MLLW), against a higher high of 5.3 ft on December 17; the king tide is 1.4 ft above Mean Higher High Water (5.84 ft).

Q: Is a king tide the same as a spring tide?
A: Not quite. Every new and full moon brings spring tides. King tide is the popular name for the highest of them, usually perigean spring tides, when a new or full moon is close to the moon’s perigee.

Q: When are the next king tides in California?
A: November 24–26 and December 23–25, 2026, and January 21–22, 2027, according to the California King Tides Project.

Q: Why are king tides bigger in winter on the West Coast?
A: NOAA says West Coast perigean spring tides have their largest range near the solstices, because of the sun’s declination, and Earth is closest to the sun around January 2.

Q: How much higher is a king tide than a normal high tide?
A: The California Coastal Commission says one to two feet higher than average high tides. At San Francisco, the December 24, 2026 high of 7.2 ft is 1.4 ft above the station’s Mean Higher High Water.

Q: Does SeaWindow warn about coastal flooding?
A: No. SeaWindow shows tide predictions and coastal weather, not storm surge or flood warnings.

## Spring and neap tides explained, with 2026–27 dates

https://seawindowtides.com/spring-and-neap-tides.html

Spring tides are the larger tides around new and full moon, when the sun and moon pull in line; neap tides are the smaller tides around the first and last quarter, when they pull at right angles (NOAA). The biggest range often lags the moon phase: from NOAA harmonic constants, the age of phase inequality is about 36 hours at Boston, 26 hours at Charleston and 8 hours at San Francisco. In NOAA predictions for Boston 8443970 (retrieved November 19, 2026), the daily range in the lunar month from December 8, 2026 ran from 7.8 ft on December 17 (first quarter) to 13.5 ft on December 25, two days after the full moon. Moon phase times from the US Naval Observatory, in UTC.

Q: Do spring tides only happen in spring?
A: No. The name comes from the tide “springing forth”. Spring tides come twice a month, all year.

Q: How long after a full moon is the biggest tide?
A: It depends on the station. From NOAA’s harmonic constants the lag is about 36 hours at Boston, 26 hours at Charleston and 8 hours at San Francisco.

Q: How much bigger are spring tides than neap tides?
A: It varies by place and month. At Boston, NOAA predicts a daily range of 7.8 ft on December 17, 2026 and 13.5 ft on December 25.

Q: Are tidal currents stronger at spring tides?
A: Yes. NOAA calls the strong currents at new and full moon spring currents, and the weak ones at the quarters neap currents.

Q: Is a king tide a spring tide?
A: Yes, an extra-large one: usually a perigean spring tide, when a new or full moon coincides with the moon’s closest approach.

## Best tide for tide pooling: how low, when, and how to find minus tides

https://seawindowtides.com/best-tide-for-tide-pooling.html

The best tide for tide pooling is a minus tide (a low below zero on a NOAA table, which uses Mean Lower Low Water) in daylight; the National Park Service at Point Reyes advises arriving at least an hour before low tide and leaving no later than an hour after it. NOAA predictions for Monterey 9413450, retrieved November 19, 2026: December 2026 has 18 minus low tides, all between 1:58 PM and 8:10 PM; eight fall before sunset (USNO), the lowest −1.7 ft at 4:19 PM on December 23, while the month’s lowest, −1.8 ft at 5:06 PM on December 24, comes after sunset. In June 2027 the lowest tides fall in the early morning, down to −1.8 ft at 6:47 AM on June 6.

Q: What is a minus tide?
A: A low tide predicted below zero on the tide table. In the US, zero is Mean Lower Low Water, so a −1.5 ft tide is 1.5 ft below the average of the lowest daily tides.

Q: How low does the tide need to be for tide pooling?
A: Lower is better. The National Park Service recommends minus tides; at Monterey in December 2026, the lowest daylight tides reach −1.4 to −1.7 ft.

Q: How long before low tide should I arrive?
A: At least an hour before the predicted low, and leave no later than an hour after it, as the Park Service advises at Point Reyes.

Q: Why are the best low tides in the afternoon in winter?
A: On the US West Coast the lowest tides fall in the afternoon and evening in winter and the early morning in summer, as the Monterey predictions show. Cabrillo National Monument says its fall and winter low tides coincide with park hours.

Q: Can I take shells or animals from tide pools?
A: Leave them. NOAA says collecting intertidal species is illegal in many areas.

## Best tide for fishing: incoming, outgoing and slack water

https://seawindowtides.com/best-tide-for-fishing.html

The usual rule of thumb is to fish moving water, the incoming (flood) or outgoing (ebb) tide, rather than slack water, but NOAA warns that the timing of slack water and maximum current relative to high and low tide is unique to each location. Worked example, NOAA predictions retrieved November 19, 2026 for December 26, 2026: Charleston 8665530 low −1.1 ft at 3:08 AM, high 6.3 ft at 9:34 AM, low −0.6 ft at 3:56 PM, high 5.1 ft at 10:03 PM (MLLW); rule of twelfths puts the fastest rise at 5:17–7:25 AM; NOAA current predictions off Fort Sumter give maximum flood 2.2 knots at 6:23 AM, maximum ebb 3.1 knots at 1:20 PM, and slack 27–40 minutes after each high and low. On the neap day of December 16 the maximum current was 1.8 knots. Solunar windows are estimates and do not predict catches.

Q: Is an incoming or outgoing tide better for fishing?
A: It depends on the spot. Both are moving water. On flats the flood brings back depth; at an inlet the ebb drains the bay through a narrow gap. Your own records from that spot are the best guide.

Q: Is slack tide bad for fishing?
A: Not always. With little current less water moves past you, but slack can be the easiest time to hold bait near the bottom. It does not always come at high or low tide.

Q: Does the moon affect fishing?
A: The moon drives the tides, and spring tides move more water. Solunar periods are a separate idea; SeaWindow shows them as estimates that do not predict catches.

Q: Does SeaWindow show tidal currents?
A: No. It shows tide heights and times. For current speed and slack water, use NOAA’s tidal current predictions.

Q: How do I find the fastest-moving part of the tide?
A: By the rule of twelfths, the water level rises or falls fastest in the middle two sixths between a low and a high. The tide height calculator works it out from two tides.

## When is high tide? Why it’s about 50 minutes later each day

https://seawindowtides.com/when-is-high-tide.html

On most coasts there are two high tides about 12 hours 25 minutes apart, and high tide comes about 50 minutes later each day, because a lunar day lasts 24 hours 50 minutes (NOAA). Worked example, NOAA predictions for Boston 8443970 retrieved November 19, 2026: the daytime high moves from 9:22 AM on November 23, 2026 to 2:38 PM on November 29, between 47 and 59 minutes later each day (53 minutes on average); November 26 has only one high tide. Pensacola 8729840, with a diurnal tide, has one high a day (1.6 ft at 9:14 PM on November 23) and none on November 26.

Q: How many high tides are there in a day?
A: Usually two, about 12 hours 25 minutes apart. Some coasts, such as many parts of the Gulf of Mexico, have one. Because the tide cycle runs on a 24-hour 50-minute lunar day, some calendar days have only one high.

Q: Why is high tide about 50 minutes later each day?
A: A lunar day lasts 24 hours 50 minutes, so Earth takes about 50 extra minutes each day to bring the same spot back under the moon.

Q: Is high tide at the same time everywhere?
A: No. Each station has its own times. In San Francisco Bay, NOAA predicts highs at Coyote Point Marina 42 minutes after the Golden Gate.

Q: Can there be only one high tide in a day?
A: Yes. In Boston on November 26, 2026, NOAA predicts one high, at 11:49 AM; the next is just after midnight. On diurnal coasts one high a day is normal.

Q: Where can I see the next high tide?
A: In SeaWindow, the Today screen shows Next high and Next low for the station you choose, with its distance and source.
